source.title: ClimaX: A foundation model for weather and climate
source.authors: Tung Nguyen; J. Brandstetter; Ashish Kapoor; Jayesh K. Gupta; Aditya Grover

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates scaling behavior in weather forecasting, a new domain, using ClimaX data, model-capacity, and resolution sweeps.
record.gate_note: Section 4.5 reports downstream forecasting RMSE against pretraining data size and model capacity, and compares forecasting at two data resolutions. It does not fit power laws or test language-model cross-entropy, small-run extrapolation, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. The numerical curves in Figures 11 and 12 are figure-only; the text describes their overall trends and exceptions.
record.test_reason: Section 4.5 runs a small scaling sweep for a weather Vision Transformer (ClimaX), a non-text setting. It varies pretraining data (1 to 5 CMIP6 datasets) and embedding size (128 to 1024) and reports 3-day ERA5 forecasting RMSE. These results bear only on V5 (scaling outside text pretraining). No curve is fitted, and the values are figure-only, so the power-law form V5 names cannot be read from them.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors report 'promising scaling laws': the two largest models improve consistently with more pretraining data and model size, while the two smallest gain little or are hurt. Higher resolution improves forecasting except for T2m at 1 and 3 days, despite a larger patch size. They do not fit any scaling law; 'scaling laws' here means qualitative trends.
record.recipe_differences: Uses ClimaX weather forecasting, RMSE and ACC, and finite data/model/resolution sweeps; it does not use language-model held-out cross-entropy or fit the original parameter, token, and compute power laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Data/model scaling differs by model capacity: the two larger models improve consistently with more data, while the two smaller models gain little or sometimes worsen. Resolution comparisons have exceptions for T2m at 1 day and 3 days.

fits_no_version.finding: A weather ViT shows monotone (not fitted) gains with pretraining data for larger models (D=512/1024). Smaller models (D=128/256) plateau or worsen. Larger models are more data-efficient.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In non-text foundation models, downstream error decreases with pretraining data only once model capacity is sufficient.

fits_no_version.finding: A model pretrained and finetuned at 1.40625° beats the 5.625° model on RMSE and ACC, except T2m at 1 and 3 days. The comparison is confounded by different patch sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weather-model forecasting skill improves with input grid resolution, as a separate scaling axis.

record.problems: The scaling results are presented in plots without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The study does not fit scaling exponents or test extrapolation, and its data-size sweep covers 1 to 5 CMIP6 datasets.
record.rows_left_out: None of the scaling-analysis results were left out. Other downstream benchmark comparisons are not scaling results.

untested.parts: Whether forecasting error follows a power law in parameters, data or compute: no fit, only five data sizes, figure-only values. Compute scaling is not tested.
No extrapolation from fitted small runs.
Depth and width at fixed parameter count are not varied; only embedding dimension changes, which alters size.
No language-model downstream tasks, and no relation to pretraining loss.
No exponents or fitting choices compared.

missing.what: Parameter counts for the four embedding sizes (only D is given; depth is fixed at 8 layers per Table 4), and the GB data sizes on the x-axis.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked everything to V6. V6 concerns downstream tasks predicted from scale or language-model pretraining loss, whereas this is a weather model's own finetuned task, so the data/model sweep belongs under V5. V5 claims the same power-law form. With five data sizes, figure-only values, no fit and no uncertainty, the form cannot be determined, so no verdict is given. The small models' plateau is consistent with a capacity bottleneck and is not a challenge. The resolution rows are relinked to none and recorded under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy or power-law fits in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or parameter/token growth trends.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The study examines weather-model scaling, but does not test whether a power-law form holds in another modality or training regime.

It reports forecasting error trends with data size, model capacity, and resolution, but does not fit a predictive relationship to pretraining loss or evaluate predictability across downstream task families.
No comparison of fitted exponents, counting or fitting choices, or departures from a fitted power law.

rows.subject: ClimaX
rows.stage_stated: pretrained on CMIP6; evaluated on ERA5 forecasting
rows.operation_detail: Varied pretraining data size from 1 to 5 CMIP6 datasets and evaluated 3-day forecasting RMSE.
rows.note: The authors state that the two smaller models do not scale as well; increasing data size brings little improvement or can sometimes hurt performance. The plot shows this target separately.
rows.check: These are a weather model, not a language model, so they belong to V5, not V6. The measure is finetuned forecasting RMSE, not pretraining loss, and there are only 5 data sizes, figure-only, with no fit. The text says the D=128/256 models gain little or sometimes worsen with more data. For small models this fits a capacity bottleneck, which V5 excludes, so it is not evidence against the version.
